_note: Section 7 drafts by reader 72 (vapes: dependence, people nearby, how much less harmful), for a targeted second reading

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: In the 2013–2014 PATH Wave 1 adult survey, 156 adults who used only e-cigarettes every day and 3,430 who smoked only cigarettes every day (weighted shares of the analysis sample 4.6% and 95.4%) answered four yes/no questions. The e-cigarette group said yes less often to each (weighted, each p < 0.0001): considered themselves addicted 77.2% vs 94.0%; ever had strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9%; found it difficult in the past 12 months to keep from using where it was prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6%; ever felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5%. First use within 5 minutes of waking 15.1% vs 24.0%; after more than 60 minutes 10.9% vs 12.1%.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3
tasks.extracted: Adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group against the e-cigarette group (95% CL), adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and poverty status: addicted 6.92 (4.46–10.73); strong cravings 2.85 (1.92–4.23); difficult to refrain where prohibited 6.39 (2.85–14.32); really needed to use 3.89 (2.36–6.40). Time to first use after waking, geometric mean in minutes, adjusted (home smoking rules added): 29.16 (24.39–34.87) in the e-cigarette group vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) in the cigarette group; unadjusted 23.46 (19.47–28.27) vs 19.25 (18.25–20.30). Editors' calculation: ratio of adjusted geometric means 1.46.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Ascertainment of Study Population, 5th paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: Of the 156 in the e-cigarette group, 145 (92.9%) had formerly smoked cigarettes at the survey's established level, 10 (6.7%) had only experimented with smoking and 1 (0.4%) had never used any tobacco product. The authors state that over three quarters of the group considered themselves addicted, and that only 6.8% of adults who had ever tried an e-cigarette used one daily against 23.8% of adults who had tried a cigarette and smoked daily, so the exclusive daily comparison picks the most dependent people who vape. The groups also differed on poverty (below the poverty level 14.6% vs 35.0%) and on home rules (use allowed anywhere at any time at home 61.9% vs 26.5%).

tasks.locator: Study limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions
tasks.extracted: The authors name as limits that amount used per day could not be compared (the units for e-cigarettes and cigarettes differ), that duration of use could not be computed, that device type, liquid nicotine concentration and flavour were not analysed, that most adults who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days also used other products and were excluded, and that use was self-reported without a biological check. They call for later PATH waves and for cotinine. The design is a single survey wave, so nothing follows people over time.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies: the 2012–2013 National Adult Tobacco Survey (a representative US telephone survey, identical wording for each product) compared 124 adults who used only e-cigarettes every day with 3,963 who smoked only cigarettes every day. Each dependence symptom was significantly less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 95% CI 35.1–57.4; withdrawal symptoms 22.8%, 14.8–33.4) and not significantly different from people who smoked cigars daily (131). The committee notes that comparisons were not adjusted for prior tobacco history or demographics and that the market then held early-model devices.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 3rd to 7th paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: The committee's account of Liu et al. (2017) repeats its figures (156 vs 3,430; 77.2% vs 94.0%; 5.6% vs 28.6%) and reads it as strong evidence that dependence symptoms are fairly high among adults who only vape every day but not as high as among adults who only smoke every day. Its limits: prior tobacco history was not adjusted for (92.9% of the e-cigarette group had smoked), so group differences may reflect earlier exposure, and the item on difficulty refraining where use is prohibited is probably a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes because fewer places restrict them (61.9% of the e-cigarette group could use theirs anywhere at home, against 26.5% of the cigarette group).

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Nationally Representative Studies, 8th to 11th paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies: a separate analysis of PATH Wave 1 (437 adults who used only e-cigarettes in the past year, daily or not, and 8,689 who only smoked cigarettes) used a 16-item dependence index tested for equal validity across products. Average severity was 1.37 standard deviation units lower for the e-cigarette-only group, comparable to cigar-only and higher among daily than non-daily e-cigarette-only participants (difference 0.40 SD). 3 of the 24 items were dropped as invalid indicators and 16 were retained as having minimal or no differential validity across products. The sample overlaps Liu et al. (same survey wave), so the two are counted as one dataset.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Epidemiology › Anonymous Web Surveys of E-Cigarette Users, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies: a voluntary anonymous web survey (December 2012 to August 2014; 3,609 people who vaped every day and had not smoked in the past 30 days, recruited on vaping and medical websites; 42% reported advocating for e-cigarettes online) compared dependence on e-cigarettes with their recall of earlier smoking: mean index 8.1 (SD 3.5) vs 14.5 (3.7). E-cigarette scores were higher with longer use, larger devices with a button, higher price and a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. A second analysis of the same data (1,048 first-generation vs 3,373 advanced devices) found higher scores (8.3 vs 7.1) and a shorter time to first use after waking (38.7 vs 67.3 minutes) with advanced devices, although their liquid had a lower measured nicotine concentration (15.1 vs 19.1 mg/mL). The committee notes the sample is not representative and that recall of earlier smoking could bias the comparison.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Conclusions, Conclusion 8-1
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is substantial evidence that e-cigarette use results in symptoms of dependence on e-cigarettes, resting on several supportive findings from good-quality observational studies with very few or no credible opposing findings (symptoms of appreciable prevalence or severity; more frequent or longer use goes with more symptoms), supported by abuse-liability studies. This is the committee's judgment.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Conclusions, Conclusion 8-2
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is moderate evidence that the risk and severity of dependence are lower for e-cigarettes than for combustible cigarettes, resting on several supportive findings from fair-quality studies with very few or no credible opposing findings; chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out. This is the committee's judgment.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8 › Conclusions, Conclusion 8-3
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 8 (Dependence and Abuse Liability)
tasks.extracted: The National Academies judged that there is moderate evidence that variability in product characteristics (nicotine concentration, flavouring, device type and brand) is an important determinant of the risk and severity of e-cigarette dependence: some findings link nicotine concentration, flavouring, device generation and brand to outcomes indicating dependence risk, with very few or no credible opposing findings. This is the committee's judgment.

tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 5: Nicotine › Main findings › Nicotine dependency, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Main findings page › 5. Nicotine, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review states that there was substantial evidence from previous reports (National Academies, the Committee on Toxicity and its own 2018 report) that vaping can result in symptoms of nicotine dependency, and moderate evidence that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarette smoking and vary with product characteristics such as device type and nicotine concentration; its pharmacokinetic review is consistent with this. It adds that many scales are used and there is no consensus on the best scale for vaping dependence, which makes comparison with smoking difficult, and cites a systematic review suggesting higher nicotine concentrations might increase abuse potential and appeal. These statements restate earlier reports and are not a new independent finding.

tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 3: Vaping among young people › Main findings › Perceived addiction and urges to vape, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: In the 2021 ITC Youth survey of 16–19-year-olds in England, 52.5% of those who currently vaped felt a little or very addicted to vaping (42.8% did not) against 83% of those who currently smoked who felt a little or very addicted to smoking (14.5% did not). Urges almost daily or more: 44.5% of those who vaped (16.8% never) against 66.6% of those who smoked (urges daily or several times a day; 4.7% never). In the 2021 ASH-Y survey of 11–18-year-olds, 41.5% of those who vaped had no urges and 23.5% strong to extremely strong urges, against 24.3% and 31.4% of those who smoked. The summary page does not say the groups were exclusive or adjusted.

tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 5: Nicotine › Implications › Improved surveillance and further research, 4th to 6th paragraphs; Need for global standards and protocols, 1st paragraph; Chapter 3 › Implications › Further monitoring and research, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review states that dependence on vaping assessed in 2021 appears lower than on smoking for young people and that further research is needed on dependence by type of product, nicotine type and nicotine strength. It calls for longitudinal studies of how dependence changes with experience, for measurements across products in people who have never smoked and start nicotine through vaping, and for a global consensus on how to measure dependence so that vaping and smoking can be compared.

tasks.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, row 'Dependence and abuse liability (52)'; Box 2, same row
tasks.extracted: The Australian umbrella and top-up review (52 studies on dependence and abuse liability: 13 randomised trials, 1 cohort, 17 non-randomised intervention studies, 21 cross-sectional surveys) rates substantial evidence that nicotine e-cigarette use leads to dependence on e-cigarettes in people who do not smoke; in people who smoke, limited evidence that it leads to dependence, limited evidence that abuse liability is lower than for cigarettes or higher than for nicotine replacement products, and insufficient evidence that abuse liability is influenced by flavour and nicotine content. This is graded more cautiously than the National Academies' moderate rating for the comparison with cigarettes.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.3 Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Table 3
tasks.extracted: In 17 adults who vaped daily (9 also smoked), using three tobacco-flavoured products chosen by the researchers and with their own breath before the first puff as the control, the first breath after one puff held nicotine in all but one person (median 108 ng, up to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol in 4 of 17 (up to 127 µg; median below the limit), glycerol in none (below the limit of quantification), tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 9 people tested (total up to 77 pg as NDMA equivalent; no difference between people who also smoked and people who only vaped, p = 0.79), formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein in none of the 4 tested, and of 13 metals in 3 people only copper (up to 2.92 ng). Only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.4 Bystander Exposure, 1st paragraph; Tables 4 and 5; Methods › 2.7, last paragraph
tasks.extracted: Modelled worst-case scenarios, not measurements in any person nearby: a car (2 people vaping at 0.5 puffs a minute for 1 hour in 2 m3 with no ventilation, the bystander a child) and an office (1 person at 2 puffs a minute for 4 hours in 30 m3 with ventilation of 0.5 per hour), built from the single highest exhaled amount for each chemical and an assumed share of the inhaled amount (40% for local effects, 33% for systemic effects) appearing in the first exhalation. Modelled air concentrations (car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; nitrosamines as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3. Editors' calculation: the Table 5 values are reproduced from the Table 3 maxima and these settings.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.7 Propylene Glycol; 3.9 and 3.10 Nicotine; 3.11 Nitrosamines; Table 6; Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Margins between the modelled exposure and the level at which an effect is expected (car / office): nicotine's effect on heart rate and systolic blood pressure 2.1 / 6 (the authors say such effects should be expected in the car and cannot be excluded in the office, of a size they compare with the caffeine in 2 or 3 cups of coffee); propylene glycol airway and eye irritation 17 / 74 or 81 (cannot be excluded in the car, mild if it occurs); tobacco-specific nitrosamines and tumour risk 521 / 2,297 against the authors' threshold of 10,000 for low concern (risk cannot be excluded in the car and cannot be assessed with sufficient certainty in the office; all four nitrosamines were treated as equally potent as N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk). Local airway effects of nicotine were not expected in either scenario. Copper stayed below a tolerable air concentration.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions › Regulatory Implications; Abstract
tasks.extracted: The authors call the effects on bystanders relatively mild even in the extreme scenario, say the nitrosamine risk could be avoided if liquids had no detectable nitrosamines and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts (no citation in the passage), and describe this as the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders. The abstract states that vaping can clearly affect bystanders' health and names glycerol as an irritant, although glycerol was below the limit of quantification in all 17 volunteers. Funding as printed: Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport; the authors declare no conflict of interest.

tasks.locator: Methods › 2.7; Results › 3.5; Discussion, 3rd to 7th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Limits the authors state: only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled and the rest estimated with an assumed retention from a model developed for cigarette smoking; the highest concentration was used; the highest emissions seen probably do not represent the worst case with so few volunteers, and low-powered products probably lead to underestimation; changes of the vapour in air, nitrosamine formation from nicotine in air, and deposits on surfaces were not modelled; toxicity data are missing for most flavour compounds. Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a person nearby, and no cigarette was measured.

tasks.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 3, section on secondhand exposure to e-cigarette aerosol
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, in volunteers vaping in chambers and rooms: five adults who also smoked, two 5-minute sessions of their own devices, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) µg/m3 against undetectable at baseline and PM2.5 152 (86.8) against 32.4 µg/m3 at baseline, no change in carbon monoxide (Czogała 2014); 37 volunteers over 4 hours with cigalike and tank devices, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 with propylene glycol and glycerol up but several-fold below workplace limits, benzene, isoprene and toluene up (a 2017 chamber study); four volunteers, particles rising but lower than for tobacco smoke (Protano 2017); nine volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 against 6 µg/m3, nicotine 2.2 against below 0.04 µg/m3, with aluminium and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons also higher (Schober 2014).

tasks.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 4th paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 3, section on secondhand exposure to e-cigarette aerosol
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, in real homes: one 60-minute sampling in a vaping household found small real-time rises in PM2.5 coinciding with vaping, but a median (9.88 µg/m3) similar to the non-vaping home (8.32; Fernández 2015); in a second home study, median air nicotine 0.11 against 0.01 µg/m3, salivary cotinine 0.24 against 0.05 ng/mL and urinary cotinine 2.64 against 0.72 ng/mL were higher in homes of people who lived with someone vaping more than 2 hours a day than in control homes (all p < 0.01; Ballbè 2014; chapter 18 gives the groups: 5 non-smoking people living with someone who vaped, 24 in control homes, 25 living with someone who smoked).

tasks.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 5th and 6th paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 3, section on secondhand exposure to e-cigarette aerosol
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, at two vaping conventions particulate matter was markedly elevated, reaching levels typical of bars and hookah venues; in one, PM2.5 was still higher the day after than the day before (Soule 2016); in the other, the estimated 24-hour average PM10 was 1,800 µg/m3, 12 times the US 24-hour standard of 150, total volatile organic compounds rose during a cloud competition, and a 7-hour air nicotine concentration of 125 µg/m3 was reported, which the committee compares with bars and nightclubs (Chen 2017).

tasks.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Characteristics and Chemical Composition of Secondhand E-Cigarette Aerosol, 8th paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 3, section on secondhand exposure to e-cigarette aerosol
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, two modelling studies (Logue 2017, Rostami 2016): in a home scenario the contribution of second-hand vapour did not exceed California 8-hour reference exposure levels except with a high-emitting device (4.8 V; up to 12 µg/m3 formaldehyde and 2.6 µg/m3 acrolein); in a bar scenario, formaldehyde (mean 135 µg/m3) and acrolein (28 µg/m3) exceeded the acute 1-hour level for the highest-emitting device and voltage and exceeded 8-hour levels in several bars under less intense vaping. Health-loss estimates (disability-adjusted life years) for device and voltage combinations were lower than, but in some instances comparable to, those estimated for second-hand tobacco smoke. The committee identified no study of health effects or early biomarkers of disease from second-hand e-cigarette aerosol.

tasks.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Synthesis, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 3, section on secondhand exposure to e-cigarette aerosol
tasks.extracted: The National Academies' synthesis: all studies measuring particulate matter and nicotine (with nicotine liquids) found statistically significant increases over background, higher with more than one person vaping and extremely high at vaping conventions; two studies detected toluene and other volatile organic compounds. The committee reads this as indoor air pollution that is lower than from second-hand cigarette smoke but above the smoke-free level set out by the Surgeon General and the WHO tobacco convention; children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk, and workers at conventions may be exposed substantially. It states that no available study evaluated health effects, clinical or early biomarkers of disease, of second-hand e-cigarette exposure.

tasks.locator: Chapter 3 › Secondhand Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol › Synthesis, Conclusions 3-1 and 3-2
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML: chapter 3, section on secondhand exposure to e-cigarette aerosol
tasks.extracted: The National Academies judged conclusive evidence that e-cigarette use increases airborne particulate matter and nicotine in indoor environments compared with background (supported by chamber experiments, real-setting experiments and observational studies in homes and convention centres; markedly lower than second-hand tobacco smoke in experiments with a single person vaping; rising markedly with the number of people vaping) and limited evidence that it increases nicotine and other constituents on indoor surfaces. These are the committee's judgments.

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction from Passive Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol Compared with Combustible Tobacco Cigarette Smoke Among Non-Users, 2nd to 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, the four studies that compared people who did not smoke or vape exposed to e-cigarette aerosol with exposure to cigarette smoke: 15 people who had never smoked, in three 30-minute sessions, blood-count indexes unchanged after passive e-cigarette exposure and the antioxidant markers unchanged after any condition, while passive cigarette smoke raised white-cell, lymphocyte and granulocyte counts for at least an hour (Flouris 2012); 54 non-smoking adults at home, airborne nicotine 0.13 µg/m3 in homes with someone vaping against 0.74 in homes with someone smoking (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine 0.19 against 0.38 ng/mL (Ballbè 2014); a chamber, one-hour airborne nicotine 3.32 against 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 against 819.3 µg/m3 for e-cigarettes against cigarettes, which the committee gives as 10 and 7 times (editors' calculation from the raw means: 9.5 and 5.4 times) (Czogała 2014); nicotine on household surfaces detected in half of 8 vaping homes against all 6 smoking homes, 7.7 against 1,303 µg/m2 (Bush and Goniewicz 2015).

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction from Passive Exposure to E-Cigarette Aerosol Compared with Combustible Tobacco Cigarette Smoke Among Non-Users, Synthesis; Conclusion 18-5
tasks.extracted: The National Academies judged moderate evidence that second-hand exposure to nicotine and particulates is lower from e-cigarettes than from combustible cigarettes. The committee identified no study of intermediate or distal health outcomes of passive exposure to e-cigarette aerosol, no long-term study comparing health effects with second-hand smoke, states that the effects of the reduced exposures on health remain unknown, that even low levels of particulate matter may confer risk, and that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may still be at special risk. This is the committee's judgment.

tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Main findings page › 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure, 3rd bullet
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review's systematic review found six studies of second-hand exposure to vaping aerosol using a variety of biomarkers, none from the UK, with exposure varying greatly from people at home to people at an indoor vaping convention. Short exposures did not produce detectable changes in nicotine, volatile organic compounds or tobacco-specific nitrosamines; longer exposures during heavy sustained vaping were associated with significant increases in nicotine or in metabolites of potential toxicants. The main findings page states no significant increase in toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape.

tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 10: Respiratory diseases › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, last paragraph; Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st paragraph; Comparisons with other reports, 6th paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review concluded there was insufficient evidence on whether acute second-hand vaping affects lung function; only 2 small studies at serious risk of bias included second-hand exposure for heart rate or blood pressure, so no conclusion could be drawn. It repeats the Committee on Toxicity's conclusion that vaping is associated with some emissions of nicotine into ambient air, so that pharmacological effects of nicotine in ambient air may occur in some individuals, and says its own two small studies of short-term second-hand exposure did not allow clear conclusions.

tasks.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, row 'Environmental hazards with health implications (25)'
tasks.extracted: The Australian review rates conclusive evidence of increased airborne particulate matter in indoor environments with e-cigarette use, limited evidence of increased airborne nicotine and of nicotine and cotinine on indoor surfaces, insufficient evidence of increased air levels of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, propylene glycol, volatile organic compounds and carbonyls, and, in the same row, insufficient evidence that the environmental hazards are of a level hazardous to human health. Authors' judgments; Box 2 counts 25 studies for environmental hazards.

tasks.locator: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review's authors recall that their 2015 report estimated vaping to be at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful to the person), a statement offered to help the public and professionals grasp the size of the gap. They write that summarising relative risks across many products, behaviours and biomarkers can be simplistic and misread; that, on the evidence reviewed, they judge the at-least-95% estimate still broadly accurate for the short and medium term; that it may now be more fitting to summarise their findings with their other firm statement, that vaping carries only a small share of smoking's risks; and that this does not mean vaping is free of risk, particularly for people who have never smoked. They add that the size of this gap is not reflected in current public perceptions. The pages read give no source or calculation for the 2015 figure. This is the authors' judgment on an estimate from their own earlier report.
tasks.quote: vaping poses only a small fraction of the risks of smoking

tasks.locator: Main findings page › 2.1 Overall conclusions; 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure; 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review's overall conclusions, on the evidence it reviewed: in the short and medium term vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks; it is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked; evidence is mostly limited to short and medium term effects, so studies of vaping for more than 12 months are needed; more standardised methods in future studies would improve interpretation. Biomarkers of toxicant exposure: significantly lower exposure to harmful substances from vaping than from smoking, as shown by biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions; similar or higher exposure than with not using nicotine products; no significant increase of toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape. Biomarkers of potential harm: the team could draw only limited conclusions, but better-run studies of short and medium term risks found no major causes of concern associated with vaping.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Nicotine; Volatile organic compounds; Tobacco specific nitrosamines; Other potential toxicants; Carbon monoxide; Metals
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The systematic review's biomarker chapter (60 studies of nicotine, 24 of volatile organic compounds, 28 of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, 9 of other toxicants, 33 of carbon monoxide and 10 of metals; designs, definitions and exposure periods varied and few studies were from the UK). People who vape compared with people who smoke, pooled analyses: nicotine and its breakdown products not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; volatile organic compound breakdown products mostly significantly lower in 15 analyses (acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower), with formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; nitrosamine breakdown products significantly lower in all 5 analyses (NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower in both analyses; metals mixed. People who vape compared with people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher, as expected (4 analyses); volatile organic compounds not significantly different in the pooled analyses except the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses, which cannot separate vaping from earlier tobacco use, while a randomised trial and a cross-over study suggest levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine; metals mostly higher; carbon monoxide similar to non-use in interventional studies of people who switched completely.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Evidence reviewed, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Implications › Vaping reduces toxicant exposure compared with cigarette smoking; Methodological improvements needed; Improvements in definitions needed, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review states that studies used a range of definitions, with some classing people who vape and smoke, vape occasionally or vape daily as one group; that studies with more than one time point mostly explored acute exposure (single use to 7 days) or followed people for 8 days to 12 months, so findings on vaping for more than 12 months could not be summarised; and that few studies could be pooled. Its implications: compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure associated with cigarette smoking, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because comparisons are lacking between people who smoked for many years and have quit and now vape and those who have quit and do not vape, and with people who have never smoked or vaped; past tobacco use can greatly affect many of the biomarkers and most people who vape smoked for many years before; and no difference between people who vape and people who use no nicotine could reflect insensitive measures, background exposure, or truly similar exposure.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Implications › More research needed on biomarkers of exposure among vapers, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review states that in its meta-analyses many findings were from tobacco industry-funded randomised trials conducted in confinement (closed settings such as research centres or hospitals) for periods of up to 7 days, and that future research needs to include more independent research on biomarkers of exposure in people who vape, people who smoke and people who use no tobacco or nicotine, outside confinement and with longer follow-up. The pages read do not say how many pooled results these trials make up or whether their results differ from the independent studies.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8: Biomarkers of potential harm › Main findings › Inflammation; Endothelial function, last paragraph; Implications › Need to distinguish biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review covered 41 studies (43 publications) of oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial function and platelet activation; most assessed acute vaping effects and most had methodological concerns. Inflammation: pooled cross-sectional studies showed lower blood C-reactive protein and sICAM-1 in people who vape than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this. Endothelial function: acute sessions of vaping (with and without nicotine) and of smoking produced similar short-term reductions in flow-mediated dilation, while a single randomised trial found that switching from smoking to vaping for 4 weeks significantly improved it; the review writes that acute vaping might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking, and that switching might improve endothelial function in the longer term. It concludes that most studies in the chapter cannot inform medium or long term risks through these biomarkers, and that studies are needed with people who use no nicotine as a comparison group and longer follow-up.

tasks.locator: Chapter 9: Cancers › Main findings › Toxicants and carcinogens; Cancer risks; Inflammation and oxidative stress; Cell and animal studies; Implications › Longer follow up periods are needed
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review's cancer chapter calls the exposure-biomarker studies conclusive evidence that vaping generally leads to lower exposure to many of the carcinogens responsible for the health risks of smoking (exposure, not cancer). It adds that the National Academies found no available evidence on whether the chemicals in vaping aerosols or vaping behaviour were associated with cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use; that evidence on inflammation and oxidative stress is insufficient for conclusions; that no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; and that cell and animal studies suggest vaping aerosols are not benign for people who have never smoked while also suggesting alterations in gene expression to a lower extent than tobacco smoke, though translating such studies to human risk is challenging. Its implications: studies of exposure biomarkers need longer follow-up to tell whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking.

tasks.locator: Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Heart rate; Blood pressure; Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness; Comparisons with other reports, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Implications, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review concludes that the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, but that based on the toxicant profile in vaping products and aerosols the risk is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking (an expectation, not a measured rate). It states that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; that 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute exposure studies, which cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; and that studies comparing rates of cardiovascular disease between people who use no nicotine, tobacco, or vaping products are needed. Measured: immediately after use vaping increased heart rate less than smoking; in pooled cross-sectional studies of longer vaping (at least 3 months or one year) people who vaped had lower blood pressure than people who smoked and no difference from people who neither vaped nor smoked; the longest follow-up of arterial stiffness after switching was 4 months.

tasks.locator: Chapter 16 › introductory paragraphs, 2nd paragraph; Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 1 › Issues addressed, 3rd paragraph and its list; Authors and citation
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review's closing chapter states that, despite the increase in research on vaping since 2015, weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups studied and exposure, and study designs all limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Its 61 evidence statements broadly follow the National Academies' definitions of level of evidence, and the authors write that, as the National Academies noted, the framework is a guide and a great deal of expert judgement, here by the report's co-authors, is involved. The scope left out two questions: vaping and later smoking (a Cochrane review of people under 30 was examining it) and the effectiveness of vaping for stopping smoking (covered in the series' previous report and by a Cochrane living review). The report is the eighth in a series described as independent and commissioned by Public Health England and then the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; it was led by academics at King's College London with international collaborators (eight authors are named); the pages read carry no competing-interest statement.

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, four laboratory studies compared emissions from e-cigarettes and combustible cigarettes. Using published data and assuming 15 puffs equal one cigarette, selected toxic compounds in smoke were 9- to 450-fold higher than in aerosol (Goniewicz et al., 2014). Of 150 chemicals examined, about 100 were detected in smoke and 16 were generated by one e-cigarette, and toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff in the aerosol depending on the list and puffing method (Margham et al., 2016). Smoke held about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents than aerosol or room air (Tayyarah and Long, 2014). Of 11 metals with smoke data, the aerosol of one cartomizer was higher for four (aluminium, iron, nickel, sodium), within the smoke range for five and lower for two (Williams et al., 2013). The committee's synthesis: aerosol is substantially less complex than smoke and, except for nicotine, exposure to potentially toxic substances under typical conditions of use is significantly lower (substantial evidence, Conclusion 5-3). The studies are laboratory measurements, not measurements in people.

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched from Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes to E-Cigarettes › Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure, 2nd to 11th paragraphs (Cravo; 5-day study; Goniewicz; McRobbie; Shahab); Synthesis; Conclusion 18-1
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, studies that followed people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes lasted from 5 days to 12 weeks: a 12-week trial of 420 people (urinary biomarkers of benzene, acrolein and a nitrosamine fell); a 5-day trial of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower in those who switched partly or completely; exhaled carbon monoxide down 88% to 89% in the groups that switched completely or stopped all nicotine); 20 people over 2 weeks (a nitrosamine breakdown product, NNAL, down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks); and 40 people over 4 weeks (carbon monoxide down 80% in those who only vaped and 52% in those who also smoked). One cross-sectional study compared 181 people who had used these products for a long time, in five groups: nitrosamine and volatile organic compound breakdown products were lower in people who only vaped, or only used nicotine replacement, than in people who smoked, and similar in people who smoked only, vaped and smoked, or used nicotine replacement and smoked (Shahab et al., 2017). Synthesis: all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who switched, and nicotine intake in people who had stopped smoking and were experienced at vaping was comparable to that from cigarettes. Conclusion 18-1: conclusive evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens (the committee's judgment).

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Switched… › Health Risk Profile (Carnevale; Cibella; Flouris; Wadia), Comparison of Nicotine and Toxicant Exposure (Martin), Toxicity in In Vitro and Animal Studies, 1st paragraph; Synthesis (after the animal studies); Conclusion 18-2
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, the committee found 15 longitudinal observational and cross-over studies of health outcomes in people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes (follow-up from single sessions to about two years; several retrospective record reviews). Examples: a one-year randomised trial of 300 people found no significant differences in lung-function indexes between groups defined by what people did after the trial began, except one small-airway flow measure that rose in those who quit smoking, with cough, phlegm and breathlessness falling over follow-up (Cibella et al., 2016); in 15 people white blood cell counts rose after cigarettes but not after e-cigarettes in 30-minute sessions (Flouris et al., 2012); in a cross-over study of 20 adults who smoked and 20 who did not, acute use of either product changed markers of oxidative stress and blood-vessel function, with flow-mediated dilation and vitamin E effects not statistically different between the products and the e-cigarette showing a lesser effect on three other markers (Carnevale et al., 2016); gingival inflammation increased in 20 people after 2 weeks of vaping instead of smoking (Wadia et al., 2016); and in nasal biopsies from 12 people who vaped, 14 who smoked and 13 who did neither, immune genes suppressed in people who smoked were also suppressed in people who vaped, with more gene changes and stronger suppression (Martin et al., 2016). In cell studies 21 of 27, and in animal studies 3 of 5, favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful and none found them more harmful. Synthesis: health effects of e-cigarettes are still not well understood but current evidence points to them being less harmful than cigarettes; all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in people who switched, though most studies were small; some studies found similar harm and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched to exclusive e-cigarette use; whether e-cigarettes reduce health risk still needs support from epidemiological studies and randomised trials. Conclusion 18-2: substantial evidence that completely switching from regular cigarette use to e-cigarettes results in reduced short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems (the committee's judgment).

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › opening section, 4th paragraph; Evidence Review: Levels of Evidence Available, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: As described in the chapter's opening, the committee writes that e-cigarettes have not been theoretically or experimentally proven to be safe, and that the evidence reviewed in the report suggests they may be less harmful than combustible cigarettes in at least some scenarios. It adds that, because the efficacy of e-cigarettes to actually reduce harm remains unclear, some researchers have raised concerns, citing McKee and Capewell (2015): continued use of a substance with its own potential health risks (including uncertainty about long-term risks), a possible increase in use of conventional tobacco products through starting and relapse, and questionable terms of engagement with the tobacco industry. The chapter states that epidemiological studies and randomised trials of the long-term health effects of exclusive e-cigarette use would give the strongest evidence of harm reduction and that, in their absence, the committee looks at biomarkers of disease and exposure levels. The chapter gives no overall figure for how much less harmful e-cigarettes are. The McKee and Capewell editorial itself was not read.

tasks.locator: Chapter 18 › Harm Reduction in Smokers Who Use E-Cigarettes Concurrently with Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes (Dual Users) › Synthesis; Conclusions 18-3 and 18-4
tasks.extracted: As described by the National Academies, for people who keep smoking while also using e-cigarettes (dual use) the committee found limited evidence on patterns of use and a lack of evidence on exposure and health outcomes among those who do not reduce their smoking. People with dual use did not on average smoke fewer cigarettes than people who smoked only, although e-cigarettes may help some of them maintain a reduction in smoking; the committee writes that it is very unlikely that people who do not reduce smoking after starting e-cigarettes will reduce the health risks of smoking, and that they may be exposed to additional adverse effects of e-cigarettes. Conclusion 18-3: no available evidence whether or not long-term dual use changes illness or death compared with smoking only. Conclusion 18-4: insufficient evidence that e-cigarette use changes short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems in people who continue to smoke. These are the committee's judgments.

tasks.locator: Opening section (before the first heading), 1st and 2nd paragraphs; References 1 to 3
tasks.extracted: The editorial states that in July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others (reference 1, Nutt et al., 2014, not read), concluding that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and e-cigarettes substantially less harmful, and that the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful. It adds that the authors of the 2013 work noted as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper); that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the assertion; that senior Public Health England staff emphasised the evidence underlying the figure despite its being lacking; and that much was written questioning the figure's validity in 2014 to 2016 (no source cited for the last two). All of this is the authors' account: none of the originals was read.

tasks.locator: Today's Electronic Cigarettes Are Different, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors argue that products today differ from those of July 2013 to the extent that the 2013 estimate, even if valid then, can no longer apply: many devices reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models and so make more aerosol, exposing the person vaping and people nearby to more nicotine and other toxicants and raising the chance of malfunction; there are thousands of flavours whose lung toxicity is unknown; and liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are widely marketed and are less aversive to inhale, which the authors say allows higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence. No source is given in the text for these statements; the supporting list is in an online appendix that was not read.

tasks.locator: Second headed section (harm to cells), 1st paragraph; third headed section (harm in people), 1st paragraph; references 5 and 6
tasks.extracted: The authors state that e-cigarette aerosols contain toxicants and are harmful to living cells in vitro and in vivo (volatile aldehydes, carcinogenic furans, chloropropanols and acetal compounds are named) and that animals exposed to aerosol show adverse effects, including in cardiovascular models (no source cited). For people they cite one report of airway epithelial injury in healthy young adults who smoked cigarettes occasionally and used an e-cigarette with or without nicotine (two randomised trials, Chaumont et al., 2019); state without a citation that wheezing has been associated with use and that heart rate, blood pressure and platelet activation rise while flow-mediated dilation and heart rate variability fall; and cite a one-page item in a journal supplement (reference 6, a conference abstract by its citation), which they call a preliminary report, for a possibly higher risk of heart attack and coronary artery disease in people who vape. The section headings state harm categorically; the conclusion speaks of potential harm.

tasks.locator: Electronic Cigarettes Increase Smoking Risk, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors quote the National Academies' conclusion of substantial evidence that e-cigarette use raises the risk of ever using cigarettes among young people and young adults, and argue that, to the extent that first use of e-cigarettes causes later smoking in someone who would otherwise never have smoked, vaping could be considered as harmful as smoking for that person. The statement is conditional on causation and concerns a person who would not otherwise have smoked, not the comparison of vaping with smoking in people who already smoke.

tasks.locator: Electronic Cigarette Aerosol Is Not Harmless, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors argue that differences in toxicant content between aerosol and smoke, by themselves, cannot show lesser lethality, because toxicity depends on the extent and mode of use; that propylene glycol is toxic when injected over days and that aerosols containing it and glycerol cause inflammation in human lungs (no source cited); and that, because the toxicants differ, so might the diseases. They also state that there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what diseases they may die of, and whether use hastens death, will be part of the evidence needed for valid risk estimates. The editorial offers no estimate of the size of the difference.

tasks.locator: Conclusions; Call to Action
tasks.extracted: Conclusion: the 2013 estimate, which lacked evidence, cannot be valid today and should not be relied upon further; future estimates should rest on the evidence now available and be revised as evidence accrues. The call to action calls the 95% safer estimate a factoid, unreliable information repeated until accepted as fact, and asks readers to highlight its unreliable provenance, the changes in devices and liquids, the accumulation of evidence of potential harm, the increased prevalence of use and the growing evidence that e-cigarette use is associated with later smoking. The editorial gives no alternative figure and does not weigh the evidence on lower toxicant exposure in people who switch: it is an argument, with no data, search or appraisal of the studies it cites.

tasks.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflicts of Interests
tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: US National Institutes of Health grants and the Center for Tobacco Products of the US Food and Drug Administration; the sponsor had no role in the preparation of the work. Interests as printed: two authors are paid consultants in litigation against the tobacco industry and are named on a patent for a device that measures the puffing behaviour of people who use electronic cigarettes; one of them has also, since September 2019, been a consultant in litigation against the electronic cigarette industry; another author reports personal fees from Hydra Biosciences LLC and Sanofi SA and non-financial support from GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals, outside the submitted work. No tobacco or vape industry funding of the editorial is stated.

tasks.locator: Abstract › Data sources, Data synthesis; Methods › 1st paragraph; Inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The Australian review combines an umbrella review of 8 major independent reviews published 2017 to 2021 with a top-up systematic review (searched July 2020, for studies published July 2017 to July 2020), 400 publications in all, registered in advance; the top-up studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the evidence graded with GRADE and the National Academies framework. It is based on work commissioned by the Australian Department of Health. It looked at the health effects of e-cigarettes in people and excluded animal, in vitro and biomarker studies as outside its scope, so the biomarker evidence on which the UK review's conclusion on relative harm mainly rests was not counted.

tasks.locator: Results › Health outcomes, Box 3, rows 'Cardiovascular disease (21)', 'Cancer (1)' and 'Respiratory disease (58)'; the three paragraphs after Box 3
tasks.extracted: Australian review, Box 3 (health outcome, number of studies): cardiovascular disease (21 studies): clinical outcomes such as heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death, and subclinical atherosclerosis: no available evidence; other cardiovascular outcomes in people who smoke: moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes acutely increase heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness, limited evidence of endothelial dysfunction and limited evidence that long-term nicotine e-cigarette use after switching from smoking reduces blood pressure; in people who do not smoke, insufficient evidence. Cancer (1 study): invasive cancer and pre-cancer outcomes: no available evidence. Respiratory disease (58 studies): asthma, bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: insufficient evidence in people who smoke and none for people who do not; reduced exacerbations or progression in people who smoke and switch: insufficient evidence. The review states that evidence is insufficient or unavailable on cardiovascular disease, cancer, respiratory conditions other than lung injury and most other conditions, and rated the certainty of evidence for clinical and subclinical outcomes low or very low.

tasks.locator: Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The review states that e-cigarettes are relatively new, diverse and changing rapidly, that long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current options (limited information on newer nicotine salt products). It describes confounding between the effects of e-cigarette use and of smoking as a major problem that statistical adjustment is unlikely to overcome, because older people who vape generally smoke regularly, are trying to quit or have quit, while younger people who vape often do not smoke regularly; it concludes that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify the effects of e-cigarettes and that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group. Statements that e-cigarettes are safer than smoking, and terms such as tobacco harm reduction, may be useful for the minority of people who smoke who use e-cigarettes to quit completely but are not applicable to people who do not smoke; comparisons with the effects of smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

tasks.locator: Limitations, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review rated the certainty of evidence very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes. It notes that the tobacco and related industries can influence research, so its risk-of-bias assessment took account of competing interests such as financial support from tobacco or pharmaceutical industries, and judges that risks of bias were unlikely to have large effects on its interpretation. It states that it applies the precautionary principle (exposure to an agent with uncertain effects to be avoided), which it considers appropriate when serious adverse impacts are scientifically plausible, particularly those affecting future generations. Products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were assumed to be largely nicotine e-cigarettes (Box 3 note).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The review states that a key finding of its synthesis was the general paucity of evidence on the effects of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarettes on many major clinical outcomes, including cancer, cardiovascular, metabolic, mental health, developmental, reproductive and neurological outcomes (other than seizures). It describes an English review it found after its search (reference 40, the UK review of 2022) as noting the lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and that most serious adverse events were infrequent, as focusing on comparing the effects of e-cigarette use with those of smoking and on biomarkers, and as generally finding more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes. It concludes that its findings concur broadly with those of other major reviews, including that the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review notes that in many countries dual smoking and e-cigarette use is the most frequent pattern of e-cigarette use and that the direct health impact of dual use is unknown. It writes that e-cigarettes may be beneficial for people who smoke who use them to quit completely and promptly, but that the limited evidence, their risks, uncertainty about effects on major clinical outcomes and continued smoking by most people who use them leave their overall safety and efficacy unclear. Its conclusions: strong or conclusive evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes can be harmful to health, particularly for people who do not smoke and for children and adolescents (a statement not framed against smoking); evidence for effects on most important health outcomes uncertain; people who smoke and switch completely and promptly may benefit.

tasks.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Box 4, row 'Smoking uptake (28)'; Discussion, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Meta-analyses of 25 longitudinal studies found strong evidence that young people who have never smoked and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking tobacco and to go on to smoke regularly (residual confounding cannot be excluded; the review deemed the link likely causal on Bradford-Hill criteria); limited evidence that people who had stopped smoking and use e-cigarettes are about twice as likely to resume smoking. The review reads this, with poisoning, dependence and other harms, as the main risks for people who do not smoke. This concerns the harm of starting to smoke, a different comparison from vaping against smoking, and the UK review left it out of its scope.

tasks.locator: Acknowledgements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Competing interests; Methods, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Funding and interests as printed: the review was conducted as part of an independent programme examining the health impacts of e-cigarettes, funded by the Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC); the report on which the article is based was reviewed by members of the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and staff of the Australian Department of Health and went through an independent methodological review as part of standard NHMRC processes; competing interests: no relevant disclosures. The work also provided evidence for the 2021 update of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners smoking cessation guidelines and a 2022 statement of the NHMRC Chief Executive Officer.
